title: Roar: The Most Dangerous Movie Ever Made?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck examine Roar (1981), a Tanzania-set family adventure film written, directed, and starred in by Noel Marshall, with his wife Tippi Hedren and their family, using a large pride of real lions and other big cats. The episode covers how the project began after a 1969 trip to Mozambique, the family's pet lions, the move to a compound in Acton (Soledad Canyon), the five-year shoot marked by dozens of injuries, animal escapes, cost overruns, the lack of a US distributor, the film's poor reception, its 2015 Alamo Drafthouse re-release and the "most dangerous film ever made" label, and the Shambala Preserve and Roar Foundation. A listener mail segment about a mangrove-planting shirt company closes the episode.
topics: pet lions in Sherman Oaks home

segments.title: Opening banter and listener note
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a movie edition and note a listener suggestion they had already planned.

segments.title: Introducing Roar and its legendary reputation
segments.summary: The hosts describe Roar as a 1981 film considered the most dangerous movie ever made, hard to see, with a 2015 Alamo Drafthouse re-release.

segments.title: Why Roar is considered dangerous
segments.summary: Comparison with other dangerous productions; Roar's danger came from its premise of putting actors near real, wild big cats.

segments.title: Origins: Africa trip and wildlife inspiration
segments.summary: Tippi Hedren and Noel Marshall, a married couple, were inspired by a 1969 trip to Africa, including an abandoned house with a pride of lions and a guide's account of poaching. Marshall had volunteered at the Saint Louis Zoo as a teen.

segments.title: African wildlife craze and TV influences
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1960s-70s fascination with African wildlife media, including Daktari and Wild Kingdom, and the trainers' initial warnings about the idea.

segments.title: Raising lions at home and the Acton ranch
segments.summary: The family raised a lion cub named Neil in their Sherman Oaks home, which Life magazine featured in 1971. After a city order to remove the animals, they bought a ranch in Acton in Soledad Canyon and built an African-style compound.

segments.title: Pre-break transition
segments.summary: Brief lead-in to the first break.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break with a Tippi Hedren fact about directors she worked with.

segments.title: Growing menagerie and self-financing
segments.summary: The couple collected many big cats and other animals, including an elephant, and self-financed the project by selling real estate and using Noel Marshall's Exorcist earnings. Early working titles were Lions and variants.

segments.title: Script, casting, and Melanie Griffith's departure
segments.summary: Marshall wrote, directed and starred in the film after no actor would sign on. Melanie Griffith briefly quit over injury fears, scenes were reshot when she returned, and the friend who replaced her was Ned.

segments.title: Expensive film stock and untrained animals
segments.summary: The production used multiple cameras and real film stock, which was costly. The untrained cats were filmed until they did something usable, and scenes like the elephant wrecking a boat were kept in the movie.

segments.title: Five-year shoot and injuries
segments.summary: The film took about five years to shoot with around 140 crew members and about 70 cast and crew injured. Cinematographer Yuri Degtyarev was scalped by a lion, requiring 220 stitches. Lack of trained wranglers contributed.

segments.title: Injuries to Melanie Griffith, son, Tippi and Noel
segments.summary: Melanie Griffith was clawed and needed about fifty stitches and later cosmetic surgery. John Marshall was bitten on the head. Tippi Hedren got a lion bite that caused gangrene and was thrown from elephant Timbo, fracturing an ankle. Noel Marshall was bitten on the hand and also got gangrene.

segments.title: Aging actors and the 1978 flood and escapes
segments.summary: Filming spanned years as child actors aged. A 1978 flood damaged fencing, some big cats escaped, and three lions were reportedly shot by deputies. A disease reportedly killed some cats.

segments.title: Setbacks, cost, and finishing the film
segments.summary: Floods and wildfire set back the shoot, destroying vegetation that had to be replanted. The film wrapped in fall 1979 at about seventeen million dollars, comparable to Raiders of the Lost Ark.
topics: Raiders of the Lost Ark comparison

segments.title: No US distributor and box office loss
segments.summary: No US distributor would sign the film, and it was non-union. It was shown in the UK and Ireland and grossed about two million dollars worldwide, losing around fifteen million.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break before returning to the film discussion.

segments.title: Plot summary and intended message
segments.summary: Plot is described loosely as an eccentric American scientist in Tanzania whose family arrives. The intended message about friendly treatment of wild animals is contradicted by the film's attacks, per critic Richard Brody.

segments.title: Tonal problems and Shambala preserve legacy
segments.summary: The film mixed home movie, slapstick, horror and comedy. The filmmakers later turned the compound into the Shambala Preserve and the Roar Foundation, which still advocates for animal welfare.

segments.title: Marshall's conduct, divorce, and 1985 Today Show
segments.summary: The couple divorced about a year after the film; Marshall reportedly had an anger problem and ignored a safe word from Melanie Griffith. Tippi Hedren promoted her book The Cats of Shambala on the Today Show in 1985.

segments.title: 2015 re-release, documentary, and reviews
segments.summary: Alamo Drafthouse coined the most dangerous film ever made tagline and the no animals were harmed line. Tippi Hedren was reportedly unhappy with the portrayal. An Animal Planet documentary came out in 2017. Reviews quoted include Under the Radar and Drew McWeeny.

segments.title: Shambala big cats today and Tippi Hedren's age
segments.summary: The Shambala Preserve has been whittled down to about nine big cats. Tippi Hedren is approaching her hundredth birthday in 2030.

segments.title: Hats off segment and Mangear listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts give a Hats Off to Tippi Hedren and read listener Robin's note about Mangear, a company that sells SPF shirts and plants a mangrove tree for each sale.

segments.title: Closing and contact info
segments.summary: Hosts thank Robin and give the email address for listener mail, followed by the iHeartRadio credit.
